## What the date above means

The date is the last time any page of this paper changed. It is not the date of the main analysis.

- **July 2025 to March 2026:** main analysis and writing by the authors. The GPT-5 Pro and GPT-5.2 Pro runs used in the main results were done in January 2026.
- **July 2026:** exploratory headless Codex pilot; signposting between the project sites.
- **September 2026:** corrections to numerical checks and comparisons.
- **October 2026:** AI-generated related-work note (OpenAI Codex), labelled where it appears.
- **November 2026:** provisional, AI-scored persistent-miss diagnostic (Claude Opus 5.5), added as an appendix and not yet reviewed by the authors.

Since September 2026, most changes have been made by AI agents at David Reinstein's request. AI-written material is labelled where it appears.

## Choose the right project view

- **Current working paper:** this is the authoritative version of the statistical analysis and academic presentation. It is available at [GitHub Pages](https://valentinklotzbuecher.github.io/llm-uj-research-eval/) and the [primary Netlify URL](https://llm-uj-research-eval.netlify.app/).
- **Full project workspace and grant proposal:** see the [broader project site](https://llm-uj-research-eval-project.netlify.app/) for project goals, team and funding context, earlier analysis, and appendices. Grant reviewers can go [directly to the proposal](https://llm-uj-research-eval-project.netlify.app/proposal.html). This material is retained for context and is not the authoritative source for the latest results.
- **LLM–human critique concordance:** see the [public concordance evidence site](https://llm-uj-concordance-judgments.netlify.app/) for the exploratory issue-mapping judgments and methods notes.

We are also maintaining a small **[headless Codex evaluation pilot](headless_codex_pilot.html)** as an exploratory extension. It is deliberately separated from the main API-based evidence because subscription-backed headless runs are useful for low-cost exploration but are less standardized and less directly replicable than the native API workflow.

A collaboration with [The Unjournal](https://www.unjournal.org/) (55+ open evaluation packages for global-priorities research). Funding: Survival and Flourishing Fund, Long Term Future Fund, EA Funds.
:::

## Can the model find the issues experts find?

```{r}
#| label: critique-headline-index
#| echo: false

source("scripts/analysis_checks.R")
crit_h <- critique_headline("results/key_issues_comparison_results.json")
crit_v2 <- critique_v2_headline()
crit_s30 <- critique_scaled_overlap()
```

`r critique_scaled_text(crit_s30)` Both are far above a placebo that pairs one paper's evaluations with the model's report on another paper (`r sprintf("%.0f%%", crit_s30$gpt$placebo$p)` and `r sprintf("%.0f%%", crit_s30$claude$placebo$p)`). So the model overlaps with an individual evaluator more than a second evaluator does, under both judges, though the two judges disagree on the level and no human has checked the matches yet. An earlier analysis of `r crit_h$n_papers` papers against a short curated consensus list reported `r sprintf("%.0f%%", crit_h$coverage_mean)` coverage, but that judge was GPT-5.2 Pro grading its own critiques; a blinded re-judging gives `r sprintf("%.0f%%", crit_v2$standard_cov)`–`r sprintf("%.0f%%", critique_v2_boot()$gpt$standard$cov)` at the main level, and about `r sprintf("%.0f%%", crit_h$coverage_mean)` only when any criticism of the same result counts.

[Headline figures and caveats](results_critiques.qmd#critique-headline) · [Per-paper coverage](results_critiques.qmd#fig-coverage-precision)
:::

## Related work: King and Worthington (2026) · [AI-generated]{title="Written by OpenAI Codex at David Reinstein's request. Not new empirical findings or agreed changes to the research plan."} note, October 23, 2026

@kingWorthington2026Peerless report strong AI review performance against paid rapidPeer experts. This substantially overlaps with our high-quality human comparison; our clearest distinctions concern structured research ratings, uncertainty, and proposed prospective and human–AI studies. See the [AI-generated comparison and research priorities](peerless_context.qmd#sec-peerless-context) and [discussion](discussion.qmd#sec-peerless).
:::

Peer review is under strain. Reviewers are hard to find, turnaround times are lengthening, and the system costs an estimated $1.5 billion per year in the United States alone [@aczel2021billion]. At the same time, generative AI lowers the cost of producing polished manuscripts; in at least some fields, editors report submission growth that exceeds reviewer capacity, and explicitly link this trend to LLM-assisted writing [@spitzer2026submission]. This combination creates demand for automated support in editorial and pre-submission workflows.

Commercial AI reviewer products such as Refine [@refineFAQ] and QED Science [@qedScience2026] already market automated referee-like feedback directly to authors, while disclaiming that they substitute for human peer review. Their internal architectures are not publicly documented. Other tools are open. IsItCredible, run by The Catalogue of Errors Ltd, sold automated "Reviewer 2" reports before retiring its hosted service, and has released that pipeline and its prompts as open-source code [@isitcredible; @isitcredibleReviewer2]. OpenAIReview [@openAIReview2026] is an open-source pipeline whose "progressive" method reads a paper in sequence while keeping a running summary of its definitions, equations, and key claims, at roughly $4 per paper. Meanwhile, publishers are formalizing policies that restrict reviewer use of general-purpose AI tools[^index-elsevier] while permitting controlled in-house applications for screening tasks [@elsevierAIPolicy2025; @leung2026policies]. Our study complements these efforts with a baseline: how closely the simplest possible setup—a single prompt to a frontier model, with no bespoke pipeline—matches structured expert evaluations, both in its ratings and in the issues it raises.

[^index-elsevier]: For example, Elsevier's policy states that "reviewers must not upload submitted manuscripts, or any information from them, into AI Tools" [@elsevierAIPolicy2025, Reviewers FAQ].

These developments make the evidentiary gap salient: funders, editors, and policymakers need to know when AI evaluation outputs are trustworthy enough to use, and when they are unstable, biased, or manipulable. Recent work documents three interlocking concerns.[^index-concerns] Reproducibility can be "jagged" across models and time [@thomas2026jagged], and subtle task reframings can induce systematic output shifts reminiscent of specification search [@AsherMalzahnPersanoPaschalMyersHall2026P_Hack]. Adversarial manipulation is not hypothetical: invisible prompt-injection text can inflate LLM review scores in simulated peer review [@choi2026invisible]. And even without manipulation, AI reviews tend to be less thematically diverse and less focused on interpretation and originality than human reviews [@rajakumar2026peerreview], while LLM scoring exhibits range restriction and halo effects that distort agreement metrics [@wang2025psychometric]. The most direct recent comparison is more favorable to AI: on 124 rapidPeer submissions, @kingWorthington2026Peerless find that AI reviews win every decided overall comparison against paid, carefully selected human reviews when an AI model judges, and 26 of 30 judgments by three former journal editors (see our [comparison with that study](peerless_context.qmd#sec-peerless-context)).

[^index-concerns]: @kingWorthington2026Peerless summarize a wider set: hallucinated claims and fabricated sources [@ye2024risks], failure to recognize novelty [@shin2025blindspots], bias toward prestigious authors and institutions [@macharlavasu2026justice; @hosseini2023fatigue], excessive leniency [@russolatona2024lottery], hidden-prompt manipulation [@lin2025hidden], and confidentiality breaches [@naddaf2025transforming]. Field evidence is also growing: the AAAI-26 conference added one labeled AI review to each of 22,977 papers sent for full review [@biswas2026aaai]; randomized studies examine LLM feedback to reviewers [@thakkar2026randomized] and reviewer AI-use policies at ICML 2026 [@kim2026icml]; and blinded editors at a cardiology journal rated AI reviews above human reviews on five of seven criteria [@zancanaro2026cardiology]. We cite these as King and Worthington describe them and have not yet assessed each study ourselves.

The central question we address is therefore: how reliably can frontier LLMs evaluate research, relative to expert peer review and under realistic levels of rater disagreement?[^index-priorities] We study this question in a setting designed to make "expert judgment" observable and multi-dimensional rather than implicit.

[^index-priorities]: A second, more exploratory question is how LLMs' research reasoning and priorities compare with those of human experts: which criteria and features of a paper they weight, and whether they would choose the same research to evaluate. The [grant proposal](https://llm-uj-research-eval-project.netlify.app/proposal.html) describes planned work on this, including comparing AI prioritization with The Unjournal's internal prioritization decisions.

We use [The Unjournal's](https://www.unjournal.org/) structured human evaluations as a reference signal. We prompt GPT-5 Pro—a frontier reasoning model—with the same rubric and guidelines used by human evaluators, then compare its ratings with available expert evaluations. The main run covers 60 economics and social-science working papers, with 47 human-matched papers; critique overlap is a separate GPT-5.2 Pro analysis of 12 eligible pairings. We ask whether a frontier LLM evaluation can approximate expert judgment, where systematic differences arise, and whether the model reveals characteristic AI preferences over research. GPT-5 Pro shows positive rank agreement with the human panel, alongside compressed ratings and uneven coverage of expert concerns. A paired bootstrap places uncertainty around an approximate comparison with human inter-rater agreement[^index-bootstrap]; it does not establish equivalence to an additional expert. [Appendix A](results_ratings.qmd) reports results from five additional LLMs spanning different capability and cost tiers, with sample availability varying by model. Because the model ranks papers broadly like the human panel but compresses its ratings and misses some expert concerns, it may be more useful alongside human evaluators than in place of them. Testing this directly would mean, for example, checking whether adding a model's ratings to a human panel improves agreement with held-out evaluations or with later publication outcomes.

[^index-bootstrap]: We resample papers with replacement 2,000 times. In each draw we recompute both the model–human and the human–human correlation on the same resampled papers, and take their difference after a reliability adjustment. The spread of that difference across draws gives the interval. See [Results](results.qmd) and [Methods](methods.qmd).

Our approach is minimal by design: each model receives the same PDF and a fixed rubric in a single prompt, with no iteration, retrieval augmentation, chain-of-thought scaffolding, or multi-step agentic loop. This provides a baseline for testing more elaborate evaluation procedures. Structured measurement tools,[^index-gabriel] steps that verify each flagged problem,[^index-verify] and [prompt-sensitivity controls]{title="Running the same task under neutral and differently framed prompts, and checking whether the outputs shift."}[^index-prompt] could improve performance, but added complexity could also amplify shared errors or introduce new biases. Their incremental value requires comparison on held-out papers.

[^index-gabriel]: @AsirvathamMokskiShleifer2026GPTMeasurement present GABRIEL, a package that uses GPT to rate attributes of text, and report performance generally indistinguishable from human annotators across more than 1,000 tasks. Their applications are not research evaluation; we cite the paper as evidence that carefully structured LLM rating can match human raters, not as a tested way to improve research evaluation.

[^index-verify]: @Zhang2025 treat LLMs as manuscript quality checkers that list a paper's most critical problems, scored against the stated reasons for withdrawn arXiv papers. They test single-pass checking and suggest a propose-then-verify workflow, in which flagged problems are checked again, for future work.

[^index-prompt]: @AsherMalzahnPersanoPaschalMyersHall2026P_Hack run AI coding agents on the same empirical analyses with neutral prompts and with prompts that nudge toward statistically significant results, to see whether the reported estimates shift.

The Unjournal setting is particularly well suited for this comparison. It commissions paid expert evaluations using a structured rubric covering seven percentile criteria with 90% credible intervals plus journal-tier predictions, and publishes the resulting packages openly rather than making binary accept/reject decisions—which may increase reviewer effort through accountability and transparency. The resulting ratings and critiques still exhibit substantial inter-rater variation;[^index-irr] accordingly, we treat human evaluations as a high-quality but noisy reference signal, not ground truth. The rich, multi-dimensional data allow us to compare the priorities and calibration of humans and AI models across criteria and domains, while eventual publication outcomes for journal-tier predictions provide an external validation opportunity[^index-1] enabling a human-vs-LLM horse race. Finally, The Unjournal’s pipeline of future evaluations allows for clean out-of-training-data predictions, serving as a live testing lab for prospective validation.

[^index-irr]: On the overall rating, two human evaluators of the same paper have a rank correlation of 0.33 (95% CI 0.02 to 0.59; 39 papers) and a mean absolute difference of 11.6 percentile points; see [Results](results.qmd#tbl-model-agreement-main). This is in line with journal peer review generally: a meta-analysis of 48 studies found a mean inter-rater reliability of about 0.34 (intraclass correlation or r²) and a mean Cohen's kappa of 0.17 [@bornmann2010reliability], though these measures are not identical to ours.

[^index-1]: These represent verifiable publication outcomes, not statements about the "true quality" of the paper.

## Unjournal impact: author engagement evidence

Do authors engage with and respond to Unjournal evaluations? An April 2026 tracking file covers 57 evaluations, but adjustment status had been assessed for 22 rather than the full set. Within that partly assessed snapshot, 16 papers have a recorded formal written response, at least 5 are coded as showing clear evidence of substantive revision, and 7 authors stated an intention to update. A full staff reassessment remains an ongoing goal.

See the **[full tabulation: did authors adjust their papers?](paper_response_analysis.html)** for the interactive table and public author statements. For broader context, see **[Evidence: do authors engage with evaluations?](https://globalimpact.gitbook.io/the-unjournal-project-and-communication-space/benefits-and-features/more-reliable-and-useful-evaluation/author-engagement-evidence)** in The Unjournal's knowledge base.
:::
